gloss: A set of printed or written pages bound together inside a cover.
examples: I'm reading a *book* about the Civil War.
She keeps her *books* in alphabetical order.
The *book* came out last spring.

gloss: One side of a sheet of paper in a book, magazine, or newspaper.
examples: Turn to *page* forty-two.
The article runs about six *pages*.
He folded the corner of the *page* to mark his place.

gloss: One of the numbered sections a book is divided into.
examples: The first *chapter* is slow, but it gets better.
I read two *chapters* before bed.
There's a map at the start of each *chapter*.

gloss: The stiff outside of a book or magazine that protects the pages.
examples: Don't judge a book by its *cover*.
Her photo was on the *cover* of the magazine.
The paperback *covers* are already curling.

gloss: The name given to a book, article, film, or song.
examples: I forget the *title*, but the cover was blue.
The publisher releases about forty *titles* a year.
He changed the *title* three times before it went to print.

gloss: A short section at the front of a book in which the author explains how it came to be written.
examples: She explains her research method in the *preface*.
Most people skip the *preface* and start at chapter one.
The second edition has a new *preface*.

gloss: A short introduction at the front of a book written by someone other than the author.
examples: A well-known historian wrote the *foreword*.
The *foreword* is only two pages long.
Both *forewords* praise the author's research.
contrast: Sounds exactly like *forward*; the book word is spelled fore-word, 'the word before'.

gloss: The opening section of a book or article that explains what it will cover.
examples: Read the *introduction* first so you know the argument.
The *introduction* lays out three main questions.
Textbook *introductions* are usually the driest part.

gloss: A separate opening scene that comes before the first chapter of a story.
examples: The *prologue* is set thirty years earlier.
I almost quit during the *prologue*.
Both novels open with short *prologues*.

gloss: A short final section that tells what happened after the main story ended.
examples: The *epilogue* jumps ahead twenty years.
I cried at the *epilogue*.
Some readers think the *epilogue* ruins the ending.

gloss: A list of special terms with their meanings, usually at the back of a book.
examples: There's a *glossary* in the back if the legal terms throw you.
The *glossary* defines about two hundred words.
Good textbooks have *glossaries*.

gloss: A list of the books and articles used or recommended by a piece of writing.
examples: Your paper needs a *bibliography* at the end.
I found the source in his *bibliography*.
The *bibliography* alone runs sixty pages.

gloss: A note at the bottom of a page that explains or gives a source for something above it.
examples: The best joke in the book is in a *footnote*.
Check *footnote* twelve for the original quote.
Academic writing is full of *footnotes*.

gloss: A note printed at the end of a chapter or book instead of at the foot of the page.
examples: The sources are all in the *endnotes*.
She buried the correction in an *endnote*.
Flipping back to every *endnote* is annoying.

gloss: The blank space along the edge of a printed page.
examples: He scribbled notes in the *margin*.
Set the *margins* to one inch.
The *margin* is too narrow to write in.

gloss: A block of sentences about one idea, starting on a new line.
examples: Cut the second *paragraph* — it repeats the first.
The story is only three *paragraphs* long.
Start a new *paragraph* when the subject changes.

gloss: A drawing or picture printed in a book or magazine.
examples: The *illustrations* are what sell the book.
Each chapter opens with a small *illustration*.
She did the *illustration* in pen and ink.

gloss: An artist who draws the pictures for books or magazines.
examples: The *illustrator* gets her name on the cover too.
They hired a different *illustrator* for the sequel.
Children's *illustrators* were all at the same table.

gloss: A short line of text printed under a photo or drawing to say what it shows.
examples: The *caption* got the mayor's name wrong.
Write a one-line *caption* for each photo.
Half the *captions* are missing from the proof.

gloss: A simple drawing that shows how something is arranged or how it works.
examples: There's a *diagram* on page ninety showing the wiring.
The *diagrams* are clearer than the text.
He drew a quick *diagram* on a napkin.

gloss: A drawing that shows numbers or facts as bars, lines, or slices.
examples: The *chart* shows sales month by month.
Put the numbers in a *chart* so people can see the trend.
All three *charts* use the same scale.

gloss: One particular version of a book or newspaper as it was printed at a given time.
examples: This is the third *edition*, with two new chapters.
The story ran in the evening *edition*.
Early *editions* of the novel are worth a lot.
contrast: Close to *addition* (ə-DISH-uhn); the book word starts with a clear short i.

countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings
gloss: One book in a set of several, or how loud a sound is.
examples: The dictionary comes in twelve *volumes*.
Turn the *volume* down a little.
She pulled the first *volume* off the shelf.

gloss: A book with a soft, bendable paper cover.
examples: Wait for the *paperback* — it's twenty dollars cheaper.
I keep a beat-up *paperback* in my bag.
The airport store sells mostly *paperbacks*.

gloss: A book bound with stiff board covers.
examples: The *hardcover* comes out in October.
She collects first-edition *hardcovers*.
I'd rather have the *hardcover* for a book I'll keep.
contrast: American *hardcover*; the British say *hardback*.

gloss: The stitching and glue that hold a book's pages inside its cover.
examples: The *binding* cracked the first time I opened it.
Old leather *bindings* line the top shelf.
Cheap *binding* is why the pages fall out.

gloss: A short piece of praise or description printed on a book's cover to sell it.
examples: The *blurb* on the back calls it 'unforgettable.'
Her editor asked three novelists for *blurbs*.
Don't trust the *blurb* — read the first page.

gloss: The text of a book as the author wrote it, before it is printed.
examples: She sent the *manuscript* to her agent in March.
The *manuscript* came back covered in red ink.
Publishers get thousands of unsolicited *manuscripts*.

gloss: One single example of a book, magazine, or record out of many printed.
examples: The book sold two million *copies*.
Can I borrow your *copy* of the report?
There's a signed *copy* in the window.

gloss: The legal right to control who may print or use a piece of writing, music, or art.
examples: The publisher holds the *copyright*.
The *copyright* on those songs expires next year.
You can't reprint the photo without clearing the *copyright*.

gloss: A line at the front of a book saying it is written in honor of someone.
examples: The *dedication* reads 'For my mother.'
He put a joke in the *dedication*.
Her first two books had the same *dedication*.

gloss: A small mistake in typing or printing, like a wrong or missing letter.
examples: There's a *typo* in the headline.
I found six *typos* on the first page alone.
It's just a *typo* — I meant 'their.'

gloss: Someone who reads a text before printing to catch mistakes.
examples: A good *proofreader* would have caught that.
The magazine laid off its last two *proofreaders*.
She works nights as a *proofreader*.

gloss: A particular design of printed or on-screen letters.
examples: Use a bigger *font* — I can't read that.
The book is set in a classic serif *font*.
She has hundreds of *fonts* on her laptop.

gloss: A particular style of printed letters, such as the one a book is set in.
examples: The whole book uses one *typeface*.
They picked a heavier *typeface* for the headlines.
He can name most *typefaces* on sight.

gloss: A company or person that produces and sells books, magazines, or newspapers.
examples: Her *publisher* moved the release date to fall.
Three *publishers* turned the book down.
The *publisher* paid a big advance for it.

gloss: Something printed and offered to the public, or the act of putting it out.
examples: The article appeared in a small medical *publication*.
The book's *publication* was delayed a year.
He writes for several *publications*.

gloss: The business of producing books, magazines, and newspapers.
examples: She's worked in *publishing* for twenty years.
*Publishing* has changed completely since e-books.
He left law for *publishing*.

gloss: Newspapers and the reporters who work for them, taken as a whole.
examples: The *press* was waiting outside the courthouse.
The mayor rarely talks to the *press*.
The movie got terrible *press*.

gloss: The process of making words and pictures on paper by machine.
examples: *Printing* costs went up again this year.
The book is at the *printing* stage now.
Color *printing* is what makes it expensive.

gloss: A long made-up story published as a book.
examples: He's writing his second *novel*.
The *novel* is set in Chicago in the 1920s.
She's read all of his *novels* twice.

gloss: A story longer than a short story but shorter than a novel.
examples: It's really a *novella*, not a novel.
The book collects two *novellas*.
Her *novella* runs about a hundred pages.

gloss: A writer of novels.
examples: She's a *novelist* who also teaches writing.
Two well-known *novelists* spoke at the festival.
He quit his job to become a *novelist*.

gloss: Writing about people and events that are made up rather than real.
examples: I read mostly *fiction* on vacation.
The *fiction* section is upstairs.
She writes both *fiction* and essays.

gloss: Writing about real people, events, and facts.
examples: His last three books were *nonfiction*.
*Nonfiction* outsells fiction in this store.
She won a prize for narrative *nonfiction*.

gloss: A book that tells the story of a real person's life, written by someone else.
examples: I'm halfway through a *biography* of Lincoln.
The *biography* runs almost nine hundred pages.
He's written *biographies* of three presidents.

gloss: The story of a person's life written by that person.
examples: Her *autobiography* came out just after she retired.
He's working on an *autobiography*.
Celebrity *autobiographies* sell well at Christmas.

gloss: A book in which someone writes about a period of their own life.
examples: Her *memoir* covers just the two years she spent abroad.
He's shopping a *memoir* around to publishers.
The store has a whole shelf of war *memoirs*.
contrast: The -oir ending sounds like 'wahr', not 'oyr': MEM-wahr.

gloss: A short piece of writing arranged in lines, often with rhythm or rhyme.
examples: She read a *poem* at the wedding.
The magazine prints two *poems* an issue.
He wrote the *poem* in about ten minutes.

gloss: Someone who writes poems.
examples: He's a *poet* and a translator.
Four *poets* are reading tonight.
She was the first *poet* he ever met.

gloss: A book collecting pieces by several different writers.
examples: Her story is in an *anthology* of new American writing.
We used a poetry *anthology* in class.
He edits *anthologies* for a living.

gloss: A book used for studying a subject in school or college.
examples: The chemistry *textbook* costs two hundred dollars.
We're on chapter nine of the *textbook*.
Used *textbooks* are half price.

gloss: A book or app that lists words with their meanings and pronunciations.
examples: Look it up in the *dictionary*.
This *dictionary* gives American pronunciations.
She keeps two *dictionaries* on her desk.

gloss: A book or website with articles on many subjects, arranged by topic or letter.
examples: My grandparents had a whole *encyclopedia* in the living room.
He treats that man like a walking *encyclopedia*.
Printed *encyclopedias* are almost gone now.
contrast: American spelling *encyclopedia*; the British write *encyclopaedia*.

gloss: A book of maps.
examples: There's a road *atlas* in the glove compartment.
He gave her a world *atlas* for her birthday.
The library keeps the old *atlases* behind glass.

gloss: A book published once a year with facts, dates, and tables.
examples: My grandfather planted by the *almanac*.
The sports *almanac* lists every record.
He keeps thirty years of *almanacs* in the basement.

gloss: A book or list showing all the items a company or library has.
examples: The seed *catalog* came in the mail again.
Search the library *catalog* by author.
They mail out two *catalogs* a year.
contrast: American spelling *catalog*; the British write *catalogue*.

gloss: A thin booklet of a few folded pages, usually giving information about one subject.
examples: The nurse handed me a *pamphlet* about the medication.
Volunteers were passing out *pamphlets* on the corner.
The *pamphlet* explains how to register to vote.

gloss: A single printed sheet handed out to give information or advertise something.
examples: Someone stuck a *leaflet* under my windshield wiper.
The clinic prints *leaflets* in four languages.
She read the *leaflet* twice and threw it out.

gloss: A small printed sheet advertising an event or business.
examples: We put up *flyers* all over campus.
A kid handed me a *flyer* for a pizza place.
The *flyer* had the wrong date on it.
contrast: Also spelled *flier* in American English; both are correct.

gloss: A magazine or book that tells a story in drawn panels.
examples: He spent his allowance on *comics*.
The *comic* came out every Wednesday.
There's a *comic* shop two blocks over.

gloss: A funny drawing in a newspaper or magazine, or a short animated film.
examples: The *cartoon* on the editorial page made me laugh out loud.
The kids watch *cartoons* on Saturday morning.
He draws a weekly *cartoon* for the paper.

gloss: A book that sells in very large numbers.
examples: Her first novel was a surprise *bestseller*.
The store stacks the *bestsellers* by the door.
It's been a *bestseller* for thirty weeks.

gloss: A short piece of writing giving the author's thoughts on one subject.
examples: He published an *essay* about his father in a magazine.
The collection has twenty-two *essays*.
Her *essay* on privacy got a lot of attention.
contrast: Stress the first syllable for the noun: ES-ay.

gloss: A short piece taken out of a longer book, article, or speech.
examples: The magazine ran an *excerpt* from her new book.
He read a short *excerpt* at the signing.
The website posts *excerpts* every Friday.
contrast: Noun EK-surpt with the stress on the first syllable; the verb is often ek-SURPT.

gloss: The series of events that make up a story.
examples: The *plot* falls apart in the last act.
Don't tell me the *plot* — I haven't seen it.
Both books have almost identical *plots*.

gloss: A person in a book, movie, or TV show.
examples: The main *character* is a retired detective.
There are too many *characters* to keep straight.
She's my favorite *character* on the show.

gloss: The voice that tells a story in a book, film, or audiobook.
examples: The *narrator* turns out to be lying.
The audiobook has a great *narrator*.
The novel switches between three *narrators*.

gloss: A type of book, film, or music with its own typical style and subject.
examples: Horror isn't really my *genre*.
The book jumps between two *genres*.
Mystery is the best-selling *genre* in the store.
contrast: Starts with the 'zh' sound of the s in *measure*, not a hard g.

gloss: A book or film that continues the story of an earlier one.
examples: The *sequel* wasn't as good as the first one.
They're already shooting two *sequels*.
She's writing a *sequel* to her debut novel.

gloss: A book or film about what happened before the story of an earlier one.
examples: The *prequel* explains how they met.
Nobody asked for a *prequel*.
The series has three sequels and one *prequel*.

gloss: A film, play, or show made from a book or other existing work.
examples: The film *adaptation* cuts half the book.
There have been four *adaptations* of that novel.
She's writing a stage *adaptation*.

gloss: A version of a text put into another language.
examples: I read it in *translation*, not in the original.
There are three English *translations* of the poem.
The new *translation* is much easier to read.

gloss: Money paid to an author or musician for each copy of their work that sells.
examples: She still gets *royalties* from her first book.
The contract sets the *royalty* at ten percent.
His *royalties* barely cover the rent.

gloss: The act of using someone else's writing or ideas as if they were your own.
examples: He was fired for *plagiarism*.
The paper ran a correction after the *plagiarism* came to light.
The school treats *plagiarism* as a serious offense.

gloss: The practice of blocking or cutting parts of books, films, or news.
examples: The editors called it *censorship*.
*Censorship* of the press is banned by the constitution.
She wrote a book about wartime *censorship*.

gloss: The group of people who read a particular paper, magazine, or writer.
examples: The magazine has a *readership* of two million.
Their *readership* is mostly under thirty.
The paper lost half its *readership* in a decade.

gloss: A person who reads a book, paper, or website.
examples: *Readers* wrote in by the hundreds.
She's a slow but careful *reader*.
The column has loyal *readers*.

gloss: A building or room where books are kept and lent out.
examples: The *library* closes at six on Sundays.
I got the book from the public *library*.
The city runs eleven branch *libraries*.

gloss: A shop that sells books.
examples: There's a used *bookstore* on Fifth Street.
She does a reading at the *bookstore* tonight.
Half the *bookstores* downtown have closed.
contrast: American *bookstore*; the British say *bookshop*.

gloss: A shelf or piece of furniture for holding books.
examples: The *bookshelf* is about to collapse.
He built the *bookshelves* himself.
There's a gap on the *bookshelf* where it used to be.
contrast: Irregular plural: one *bookshelf*, two *bookshelves*.

gloss: A recording of a book being read aloud.
examples: I listen to *audiobooks* on my commute.
The *audiobook* is fourteen hours long.
The author reads her own *audiobook*.

gloss: A book you read on a screen instead of on paper.
examples: The *ebook* is three dollars cheaper.
I have about four hundred *ebooks* on this thing.
The *ebook* came out the same day as the hardcover.

gloss: A set of large printed sheets sold daily or weekly with news in it.
examples: He still reads a *newspaper* with breakfast.
The story ran in every *newspaper* in the state.
Local *newspapers* are shutting down all over.
contrast: Americans say NOOZ; the British say NYOOZ.

gloss: A thin publication with photos and articles, printed weekly or monthly.
examples: There's a stack of old *magazines* in the waiting room.
She writes for a food *magazine*.
The *magazine* comes out on the first of the month.
contrast: Americans usually stress the first syllable, MAG-uh-zeen; the British stress the last.

gloss: A serious magazine for a profession or field of study, or a private diary.
examples: The findings appeared in a medical *journal*.
The library subscribes to over two hundred *journals*.
She keeps a *journal* by her bed.

gloss: The work of gathering and reporting news.
examples: She studied *journalism* in college.
That series was excellent *journalism*.
*Journalism* pays badly and always has.

gloss: The room or department where reporters and editors put the news together.
examples: The *newsroom* went quiet when the call came in.
He spent thirty years in that *newsroom*.
*Newsrooms* are a third the size they used to be.

gloss: A piece of writing about one subject in a newspaper, magazine, or website.
examples: Did you read the *article* about the bridge?
She's filed three *articles* this week.
The *article* is behind a paywall.

gloss: The title printed in large type above a news story.
examples: The *headline* was bigger than the story deserved.
He only reads the *headlines*.
That verdict made *headlines* across the country.

gloss: The line naming the reporter who wrote an article.
examples: Her *byline* was on the front page.
He got his first *byline* at nineteen.
The piece ran with two *bylines*.

gloss: An article giving the opinion of the newspaper itself rather than a reporter.
examples: The paper ran an *editorial* against the tax.
He writes most of the *editorials*.
The *editorial* called for the chief to resign.

gloss: A writer with a regular signed piece in a paper or magazine.
examples: She's a sports *columnist* for the local paper.
Two *columnists* quit over the decision.
The *columnist* apologized the next week.
contrast: The n is silent in *column* but pronounced in *columnist*: KAH-luhm-nist.

gloss: A writer who supplies pieces to a magazine or site without being on staff.
examples: She's a regular *contributor* to the food section.
The masthead lists forty *contributors*.
They pay *contributors* by the word.

gloss: Someone whose job is to find out about news and write or talk about it.
examples: A *reporter* called the house twice.
*Reporters* were camped outside all week.
He's been a crime *reporter* for ten years.

gloss: A reporter who covers one place or subject for a paper or network.
examples: Our White House *correspondent* has the story.
She spent four years as a foreign *correspondent*.
Two *correspondents* were pulled out of the country.

gloss: Someone whose job is to judge books, films, food, or art in public.
examples: The film *critic* gave it two stars.
*Critics* loved it; nobody went to see it.
She's the restaurant *critic* for the paper.

gloss: A person who writes an opinion piece about a new book, film, or product.
examples: One *reviewer* called it the book of the year.
*Reviewers* got advance copies in June.
The *reviewer* clearly hadn't finished it.

gloss: A long newspaper or magazine article about one subject, rather than straight news.
examples: She's writing a *feature* on the housing shortage.
The Sunday *feature* runs about five thousand words.
He does mostly *features* now, not daily reporting.

gloss: The reporting a story gets in newspapers, on TV, or online.
examples: The trial got wall-to-wall *coverage*.
Local *coverage* of the storm was excellent.
There was almost no *coverage* of the vote.

gloss: An important news story that one reporter gets before anyone else.
examples: That story was a real *scoop*.
She got the *scoop* from a source at city hall.
The paper has had two big *scoops* this month.

gloss: A person or document that gives a reporter information.
examples: He won't name his *source*.
Two *sources* confirmed the story.
A *source* inside the company leaked the memo.

gloss: Someone's exact words repeated in a story or book.
examples: That *quote* was taken out of context.
The article is just three *quotes* and no facts.
Can I use that as a *quote*?

gloss: A group of words taken from a book or speech and repeated exactly.
examples: The chapter opens with a *quotation* from Twain.
He collects *quotations* in a little notebook.
That *quotation* is usually misattributed.

gloss: A short article about someone's life printed after they die.
examples: I read his *obituary* in the paper.
She writes *obituaries* for the Sunday edition.
The *obituary* left out his first marriage.

gloss: A word puzzle in a grid, printed in most newspapers.
examples: He does the *crossword* in pen.
Sunday's *crossword* took me two hours.
She saves the *crosswords* for the plane.

gloss: A short forecast for people born under each star sign, printed in papers.
examples: My *horoscope* said to avoid big decisions.
She reads the *horoscope* first, then the news.
The *horoscopes* are on the back page.

gloss: A small-format newspaper full of celebrity news and short, dramatic stories.
examples: The *tabloids* ran the photo for a week.
You can't believe anything in that *tabloid*.
She sold her story to a *tabloid*.

gloss: A small open stall on a street or in a station that sells papers and magazines.
examples: I grabbed a paper at the *newsstand*.
The magazine sells better on *newsstands* than by mail.
There used to be a *newsstand* on every corner.

gloss: A short regular report emailed or mailed to members or subscribers.
examples: Sign up for our weekly *newsletter*.
The school sends a *newsletter* home every Friday.
I get too many *newsletters*.

gloss: A short news announcement or report, especially an urgent one.
examples: They broke into the show with a news *bulletin*.
The station runs a weather *bulletin* every hour.
The first *bulletin* said only that a plane was down.

gloss: A meeting where officials give reporters information about a situation.
examples: The *briefing* starts at ten.
She asked two questions at the *briefing*.
Daily *briefings* were cut back to twice a week.

gloss: The number of copies of a paper or magazine that are sold.
examples: The paper's *circulation* has fallen by half.
*Circulation* peaked in the eighties.
The magazine claims a *circulation* of 90,000.

gloss: Someone who pays regularly to receive a paper, magazine, or service.
examples: The site has 40,000 paying *subscribers*.
*Subscribers* get the article a day early.
She's been a *subscriber* since 1998.

gloss: A magazine or journal that comes out at regular times.
examples: The *periodicals* are on the second floor.
The library keeps back issues of every *periodical*.
It's a quarterly *periodical* for teachers.

gloss: A publication that gives short versions of longer articles or news.
examples: I get a weekly *digest* of the top stories.
The *digest* is only four pages.
Both *digests* covered the same three stories.
contrast: Noun DY-jest with the stress up front; the verb 'to digest' is dy-JEST.

gloss: Newspapers, television, radio, and websites taken together as a source of news.
examples: The *media* covered the story for weeks.
She blamed the *media* for the leak.
Social *media* changed how news travels.
contrast: Originally the plural of *medium*; Americans usually treat *the media* as one thing: 'the media is.'

gloss: One numbered edition of a magazine or newspaper.
examples: The April *issue* has her interview in it.
I've saved every *issue* since the first one.
The next *issue* comes out Thursday.

gloss: The first page of a newspaper, where the biggest stories go.
examples: The scandal was on the *front page* for three days.
That story never made the *front page*.
All the *front pages* carried the same photo.

gloss: A short official statement a company or agency sends to reporters.
examples: The company put out a *press release* denying it.
Half these stories are just rewritten *press releases*.
The *press release* went out at six in the morning.

gloss: An opinion piece in a newspaper written by someone outside the paper's staff.
examples: The senator wrote an *op-ed* defending the bill.
Her *op-ed* got two thousand comments.
They publish three *op-eds* a day.

gloss: A program sent out on radio, television, or the internet.
examples: The *broadcast* starts at eight.
Millions watched the live *broadcast*.
The station lost two *broadcasts* to the storm.

gloss: A company or person that sends out radio or television programs.
examples: The *broadcaster* holds the rights to the games.
Three *broadcasters* bid for the contract.
He's been a *broadcaster* for thirty years.

countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings
gloss: The system of sending pictures and sound to homes, or the set that shows them.
examples: He works in *television*.
There's a *television* in every room of the hotel.
I saw it on *television* last night.

gloss: A single show on radio or television.
examples: It's my favorite *program* on the radio.
The *program* airs Sunday nights.
They canceled two *programs* this season.
contrast: American spelling *program*; the British write *programme* for a broadcast.

gloss: A television or radio program, especially an entertaining one.
examples: That *show* has been on for nine seasons.
She hosts a morning *show*.
We binged three *shows* over the weekend.

gloss: One separate part of a television series or podcast.
examples: The last *episode* airs next week.
There are ten *episodes* in the season.
I fell asleep halfway through the *episode*.

gloss: A short advertisement shown between parts of a TV or radio program.
examples: I muted the *commercial*.
The *commercials* are longer than the show.
That *commercial* has been running for years.

gloss: A notice or short film that tries to sell something or attract attention.
examples: There's a full-page *advertisement* on the back.
The magazine is mostly *advertisements* now.
They pulled the *advertisement* after complaints.
contrast: American ad-vur-TYZ-muhnt; the British say uhd-VUR-tis-muhnt.

gloss: A short everyday word for an advertisement.
examples: I skipped the *ad* after five seconds.
They put an *ad* in the paper for a dishwasher.
The site is covered in *ads*.
contrast: Sounds exactly like *add*.

gloss: A measure of how many people watch or listen to a program.
examples: The show's *ratings* dropped after the move.
The finale got the highest *rating* of the year.
*Ratings* decide what gets canceled.

gloss: A film or program about real events and real people.
examples: We watched a *documentary* about the flood.
She makes *documentaries* for public television.
The *documentary* runs two and a half hours.

gloss: A funny TV series with the same characters in the same setting each week.
examples: It's a *sitcom* about four roommates.
He got famous on a *sitcom* in the nineties.
They watch old *sitcoms* every night.

gloss: A serious television series, film, or play.
examples: It's a legal *drama* set in Boston.
The network ordered two new *dramas*.
That *drama* won every award last year.

gloss: A television or radio program that reports the news.
examples: The evening *newscast* leads with the fire.
She's been doing the morning *newscast* for years.
Local *newscasts* still draw big audiences.

gloss: The person whose voice introduces programs or describes events on air.
examples: The *announcer* gave the score twice.
You could hear the *announcer* choking up.
Both *announcers* worked the game.

gloss: Someone who describes or explains events on TV or radio as they happen.
examples: The *commentator* called it the play of the season.
Political *commentators* argued about it all night.
He works as a *commentator* now that he's retired.

gloss: The person who asks the questions in an interview.
examples: The *interviewer* never let him finish a sentence.
She's a tough but fair *interviewer*.
Two *interviewers* took turns.

gloss: One separate part of a television or radio program.
examples: They cut my *segment* for time.
The cooking *segment* airs after the weather.
The show is built out of six short *segments*.
contrast: Noun SEG-muhnt with the stress up front; the verb is seg-MENT.

gloss: Film or video that has been shot, especially of a real event.
examples: The station aired security *footage* of the break-in.
There's hours of unused *footage*.
The *footage* is grainy but you can see his face.

gloss: A written copy of everything that was said in a recording or hearing.
examples: The full *transcript* is on the website.
He read the *transcript* instead of watching the tape.
They released the *transcripts* the next morning.

gloss: The written words of a film, play, or broadcast.
examples: The anchor read straight from the *script*.
She's on the fourth draft of the *script*.
They send out *scripts* a week before taping.

gloss: The script of a movie, with the dialogue and the action.
examples: He wrote the *screenplay* in six weeks.
The *screenplay* is based on her novel.
She's sold two *screenplays* and neither got made.

gloss: Words shown at the bottom of the screen giving what is being said.
examples: I watch everything with *subtitles* on.
The *subtitles* were a few seconds behind.
The film is in Korean with English *subtitles*.

gloss: A voice heard over a film or commercial without the speaker being seen.
examples: The whole ad is one long *voiceover*.
He does *voiceovers* for car commercials.
They recorded the *voiceover* in a single take.

gloss: The music used in a film or show, often sold as an album.
examples: The *soundtrack* is better than the movie.
She bought the *soundtrack* on vinyl.
Both *soundtracks* were nominated.

gloss: The first public showing of a film or the first episode of a season.
examples: The season *premiere* airs Sunday.
She wore a red dress to the *premiere*.
Both *premieres* drew huge audiences.

gloss: The last episode of a series or the final part of a show.
examples: Nobody liked the series *finale*.
The season *finale* ends on a cliffhanger.
Twelve million people watched the *finale*.

gloss: A television program shown again after its first broadcast.
examples: It's just a *rerun* — I've seen this one.
They show *reruns* all summer.
The *rerun* airs at midnight.

gloss: Watching or listening to something over the internet as it arrives, without downloading it.
examples: *Streaming* killed the video store.
The show does well in *streaming*.
Our *streaming* keeps buffering tonight.

gloss: An audio program you download or stream, usually released in episodes.
examples: I listen to a history *podcast* while I run.
They started a *podcast* about local politics.
There are three hundred *podcasts* on my phone.

gloss: A website where someone posts short pieces of writing in date order.
examples: She keeps a cooking *blog*.
He posted it on his *blog* first.
A few *blogs* picked up the story before the papers did.

gloss: Someone who writes a blog.
examples: A *blogger* broke the story.
Food *bloggers* were invited to the opening.
She's a full-time *blogger* now.

gloss: Someone with a large online following who is paid to promote things.
examples: The brand hired three *influencers*.
She quit her job to be a full-time *influencer*.
*Influencers* get free hotel rooms for a post.

gloss: Sound or video that has been captured so it can be played back.
examples: The *recording* cuts off after ten minutes.
He played a *recording* of the phone call.
There are early *recordings* of her in the archive.

gloss: The crackling noise that interferes with a radio or TV signal.
examples: All I could hear was *static*.
The storm filled the radio with *static*.
The line went to *static* halfway through.

gloss: A person watching a television program or video.
examples: The show lost a million *viewers* this season.
One *viewer* called in to complain.
*Viewers* voted by text message.

gloss: A person listening to a radio station or podcast.
examples: The station has 200,000 weekly *listeners*.
A *listener* wrote in with the answer.
He thanked his *listeners* on the last show.
contrast: The t is silent, as in *listen*: LIS-uh-nur.
